NOTE

 

• In inference questions, the answer must be drawn from the passage as a whole. Options that introduce extreme words such as *always, never, anywhere, impossible* are usually incorrect, because passages rarely make such absolute claims.

question: Which of the following acids is naturally present in curd and sour milk?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lactic acid.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lactic acid is the acid naturally present in curd, sour milk, yoghurt and buttermilk. (लैक्टिक अम्ल — दही एवं खट्टे दूध में)

 

• It is produced when the bacterium Lactobacillus converts the milk sugar lactose into lactic acid during fermentation. This is what gives curd its sour taste and causes the milk protein to set.

 

• Lactic acid also accumulates in the muscles during vigorous exercise, when oxygen supply is insufficient and glucose undergoes anaerobic respiration. This is a common cause of muscle cramps and fatigue.

 

• Common natural acids and their sources:
◦ Citric acid — lemon, orange and other citrus fruits
◦ Acetic acid — vinegar
◦ Tartaric acid — tamarind and grapes
◦ Oxalic acid — tomato and spinach
◦ Malic acid — apple
◦ Formic acid — ant sting and nettle sting
◦ Butyric acid — rancid butter

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Acids taste sour and turn blue litmus red; bases taste bitter and turn red litmus blue.

 

• The pH scale, devised by S.P.L. Sorensen, runs from 0 to 14. A pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral and above 7 is basic. The pH of human blood is about 7.4, and that of gastric juice about 1.5 to 3.5.

 

NOTE

 

• Citric acid (Option 1): Found in lemon, lime and orange; widely used as a food preservative.

 

• Oxalic acid (Option 2): Found in tomato, spinach and wood sorrel; excess of it can lead to kidney stones.

 

• Tartaric acid (Option 3): Found in tamarind and grapes; it is a component of baking powder.

question: Which of the following Five Year Plans of India is also known as the Gadgil Yojana?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Third Five Year Plan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Third Five Year Plan (1961-1966) is also known as the Gadgil Yojana, after D.R. Gadgil, who was closely associated with its formulation and later served as Deputy Chairman of the Planning Commission. (तृतीय पंचवर्षीय योजना — गाडगिल योजना)

 

• Its principal objective was to make the economy self-reliant and self-generating, with emphasis on agriculture and the improvement of wheat production.

 

• The plan is generally regarded as a failure, because of the Sino-Indian War of 1962, the Indo-Pak War of 1965 and a severe drought in 1965-66, which diverted resources to defence and relief. Its failure led to the declaration of three Annual Plans (1966-1969), known as the Plan Holiday.

 

• Panchayat elections were held and State Electricity Boards and State Secondary Education Boards were set up during this plan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Key Five Year Plans for examinations:
◦ First (1951-56): Based on the Harrod-Domar model; focus on agriculture; the most successful plan.
◦ Second (1956-61): Based on the P.C. Mahalanobis model; focus on heavy and basic industries; also called the Nehru-Mahalanobis Plan.
◦ Fourth (1969-74): Aimed at growth with stability and self-reliance; nationalisation of 14 banks and the Green Revolution.
◦ Fifth (1974-79): Slogan "Garibi Hatao"; focus on poverty removal and self-reliance.
◦ Sixth (1980-85): Beginning of economic liberalisation; NABARD established in 1982.
◦ Twelfth (2012-17): The last Five Year Plan; theme of faster, more inclusive and sustainable growth.

 

• The Planning Commission was set up in 1950 by an executive resolution and was replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015.

 

NOTE

 

• Second Five Year Plan (Option 1): The Mahalanobis Plan, devoted to heavy industry.

 

• Fourth Five Year Plan (Option 3): Ran from 1969 to 1974 under Indira Gandhi.

 

• Fifth Five Year Plan (Option 4): Ran from 1974 to 1979 and was terminated a year early by the Janata Government.

question: In human beings, the exchange of gases between the blood and the air takes place in the ______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is alveoli.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The alveoli are the tiny, thin-walled, balloon-like air sacs at the ends of the smallest bronchioles in the lungs, and they are the site where the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the air and the blood takes place. (कूपिका — गैसों का विनिमय)

 

• Their walls are only one cell thick and are surrounded by a dense network of blood capillaries, so gases diffuse across easily. Oxygen passes from the alveolar air into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the alveolar air.

 

• There are roughly 300 million alveoli in a pair of human lungs, giving a total surface area of about 70-80 square metres — nearly the area of a badminton court. This vast area makes gaseous exchange highly efficient.

 

• The path of air is: nostrils → nasal cavity → pharynx → larynx (voice box) → trachea (windpipe) → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The right lung has three lobes and the left lung two, the smaller size of the left lung leaving room for the heart. The lungs are located in the thoracic cavity.

 

• The diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle, and the intercostal muscles bring about breathing. During inhalation the diaphragm contracts and flattens, increasing the volume of the chest cavity.

 

• Oxygen is carried in the blood by haemoglobin in the red blood cells, while most carbon dioxide is transported dissolved in the plasma as bicarbonate.

 

NOTE

 

• Trachea (Option 2): The windpipe, supported by C-shaped rings of cartilage that keep it from collapsing.

 

• Bronchi (Option 3): The two large tubes into which the trachea divides, one entering each lung. They only conduct air.

 

• Pleura (Option 4): The double-layered membrane covering the lungs; the fluid between its layers reduces friction during breathing.

question: The inscriptions of Emperor Ashoka were written mainly in which script in most parts of his empire?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Brahmi.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Most of Ashoka's inscriptions were engraved in the Brahmi script, which was written from left to right and used the Prakrit language in the greater part of the empire. (ब्राह्मी लिपि — अशोक के अभिलेख)

 

• The Brahmi script was deciphered in 1837 by James Prinsep, an officer of the East India Company, an achievement that opened up the study of ancient Indian history and first revealed the identity of "Devanampiya Piyadasi" as Ashoka.

 

• In the north-western regions (present-day Pakistan and Afghanistan) the edicts were written in the Kharosthi script, which runs from right to left; at Shahbazgarhi and Mansehra Kharosthi was used, while the Kandahar inscriptions were in Greek and Aramaic.

 

• Ashoka's inscriptions are classified as Major Rock Edicts (14), Minor Rock Edicts, Major Pillar Edicts (7), Minor Pillar Edicts and Cave Inscriptions (the Barabar caves, granted to the Ajivikas).

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Ashoka (268-232 BCE) was the grandson of Chandragupta Maurya and the son of Bindusara. He fought the Kalinga War in 261 BCE, described in Rock Edict XIII, after which he embraced Buddhism.

 

• The Lion Capital of Sarnath, built by Ashoka, was adopted as the State Emblem of India on 26 January 1950. The Dharma Chakra from its abacus appears on the national flag.

 

• Ashoka is referred to in his inscriptions as "Devanampiya Piyadasi" (Beloved of the Gods, of pleasing appearance). The Maski and Gujarra minor rock edicts mention his personal name, Ashoka.

 

NOTE

 

• Kharosthi (Option 1): Used only in the north-west of the empire; written from right to left.

 

• Aramaic (Option 3): Used in the Kandahar region of Afghanistan, along with Greek, for the benefit of the local population.

 

• Greek (Option 4): Also used at Kandahar in a bilingual edict, but not in the main body of the empire.

question: 'Cheraw', popularly known as the bamboo dance, is a folk dance of which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mizoram.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Cheraw is the best-known folk dance of Mizoram and is popularly called the bamboo dance. (चेरॉ — मिजोरम का बाँस नृत्य)

 

• In this dance, men sit facing each other on the ground and tap long pairs of bamboo staves open and close in rhythm, while women dancers step in and out of the closing bamboos with great precision. It is regarded as one of the oldest and most graceful dances of the North-East.

 

• It is performed on festive occasions, particularly during Chapchar Kut, the spring festival of Mizoram celebrated in March after the clearing of jungle for cultivation.

 

• Other folk dances of Mizoram: Khuallam, Chheihlam, Sarlamkai and Zangtalam.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Folk dances of the North-Eastern states frequently asked in SSC:
◦ Assam — Bihu, Jhumur, Bagurumba
◦ Nagaland — Chang Lo (Sua Lua), Zeliang, Nuralim
◦ Manipur — Thang Ta, Dhol Cholom, Lai Haraoba
◦ Tripura — Hojagiri, Garia, Lebang Boomani
◦ Meghalaya — Nongkrem, Laho, Shad Suk Mynsiem
◦ Arunachal Pradesh — Bardo Chham, Ponung, Lion and Peacock dance
◦ Sikkim — Singhi Chham, Maruni, Chu Faat

 

NOTE

 

• Nagaland (Option 1): Known for the Chang Lo and Zeliang dances and the Hornbill Festival.

 

• Tripura (Option 2): Known for Hojagiri, in which women balance on earthen pitchers while dancing.

 

• Manipur (Option 3): Home of Manipuri, one of the eight classical dance forms of India, and of the martial art dance Thang Ta.

question: The Sekrenyi festival, celebrated as a festival of purification, is associated with which tribe of Nagaland?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Angami.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Sekrenyi, also called Phousanyi, is the principal festival of the Angami tribe of Nagaland and is celebrated as a festival of purification of body and soul. (सेक्रेनी — अंगामी जनजाति)

 

• It is commonly observed on 25 February each year and continues for about ten days. It marks the beginning of the new year and, traditionally, the transition of young men from boyhood to adulthood.

 

• A central ritual is Kizie, in which a few drops of rice water are taken from the first drawn water of the village well, followed by the ceremonial bathing of the young men at the village well — the act of purification from which the festival takes its name.

 

• The Angamis are one of the major Naga tribes, concentrated in the Kohima district, and are known for their terraced wet-rice cultivation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Major festivals of Nagaland and their tribes:
◦ Moatsu and Tsungremmong — Ao tribe
◦ Aoleang (Aoleang Monyu) — Konyak tribe
◦ Tuluni and Ahuna — Sumi (Sema) tribe
◦ Nazhu — Pochury tribe
◦ Mimkut — Kuki tribe

 

• The Hornbill Festival, called the "Festival of Festivals", is held every year from 1 to 10 December at the Naga Heritage Village, Kisama, near Kohima. It was started in 2000 to showcase all the tribes of Nagaland together. Nagaland attained statehood on 1 December 1963, becoming the 16th state of India.

 

NOTE

 

• Ao (Option 1): Celebrates Moatsu in May, after the sowing is complete.

 

• Konyak (Option 2): Celebrates Aoleang in April; the tribe was historically known for headhunting and facial tattoos.

 

• Sumi (Option 4): Celebrates Tuluni in July, the festival of the greatest feasting in the year.

question: Which Indian ruler was the first to accept the Subsidiary Alliance introduced by Lord Wellesley?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Nizam of Hyderabad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Nizam of Hyderabad was the first Indian ruler to accept the Subsidiary Alliance, in 1798, shortly after Lord Wellesley became Governor-General. (सहायक संधि — सर्वप्रथम हैदराबाद का निज़ाम, 1798)

 

• Under the Subsidiary Alliance system, an Indian ruler had to:
◦ accept a British force stationed within his territory and pay for its maintenance, often by surrendering territory;
◦ accept a British Resident at his court;
◦ dismiss all Europeans of other nationalities from his service;
◦ not enter into alliances or wage war with any other power without British permission.
◦ In return, the Company guaranteed protection from external attack and internal rebellion.

 

• Order of acceptance: the Nizam of Hyderabad (1798), the Ruler of Mysore (1799, after the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War), the Raja of Tanjore (1799), the Nawab of Awadh (1801), the Peshwa Baji Rao II (1802, by the Treaty of Bassein), the Bhonsle of Berar (1803) and the Scindia (1804).

 

• The system made the Indian states militarily helpless and financially drained, and it is often described as the instrument by which the Company became the paramount power in India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lord Wellesley was Governor-General from 1798 to 1805 and called himself the "Bengal Tiger". He fought the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799), in which Tipu Sultan was killed, and the Second Anglo-Maratha War (1803-1805).

 

• The idea of a subsidiary force was not new — the French governor Dupleix had first used it in India.

 

• Another instrument of annexation, the Doctrine of Lapse, was applied by Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856); Satara (1848) was the first state annexed under it and Jhansi and Nagpur followed. Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernment.

 

NOTE

 

• The Nawab of Awadh (Option 2): Accepted the alliance in 1801 and had to surrender more than half his territory to the Company.

 

• Peshwa Baji Rao II (Option 3): Signed the Treaty of Bassein in 1802, which brought the Marathas into the system and led to the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

 

• The Raja of Mysore (Option 4): The alliance was imposed after Tipu Sultan's defeat and death in 1799.

question: The value of acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Moon is approximately how much of its value on the surface of the Earth?
solution_text:
The correct answer is One-sixth.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The acceleration due to gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth of that on the Earth. On the Earth g ≈ 9.8 m/s², and on the Moon it is about 1.63 m/s². (चंद्रमा पर गुरुत्वीय त्वरण — पृथ्वी का लगभग 1/6)

 

• The reason lies in the formula g = GM / R², where M is the mass and R the radius of the body. The Moon's mass is far smaller than the Earth's, and although its radius is also smaller, the net effect is a value about one-sixth as large.

 

• A consequence often tested: the mass of a body remains the same everywhere, but its weight (W = mg) on the Moon is only one-sixth of its weight on the Earth. This is why astronauts can leap high on the lunar surface.

 

• The Moon has no atmosphere, because its gravity is too weak to retain gases.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The value of g is maximum at the poles and minimum at the equator, because the Earth is flattened at the poles and bulges at the equator. It decreases as one goes above the surface and also as one goes deep below it, becoming zero at the centre of the Earth.

 

• Newton's law of universal gravitation: every particle attracts every other particle with a force F = Gm₁m₂ / r². The universal gravitational constant G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg², and its value is the same everywhere in the universe.

 

• The escape velocity on the Earth is about 11.2 km/s, and on the Moon about 2.4 km/s.

 

NOTE

 

• One-third (Option 1) is close to the ratio for Mars, where g is about 3.7 m/s², roughly 38% of the Earth's value.

 

• One-fourth (Option 2) and One-eighth (Option 4) do not correspond to any major body of the solar system in relation to the Earth.

question: As of 2025, which planet of the solar system has the largest number of confirmed moons recognised by the International Astronomical Union?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Saturn.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• As of 2025, Saturn has 274 confirmed moons, the largest number of any planet in the solar system — more than all the other planets put together. (शनि — सर्वाधिक चंद्रमा)

 

• In March 2025 the International Astronomical Union recognised 128 newly discovered moons of Saturn at one time, nearly doubling its count and putting it decisively ahead of Jupiter, which has about 95 recognised moons. The discoveries were made by a team led by Edward Ashton by stacking images from the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope.

 

• Of Saturn's moons, about 24 are regular and the rest irregular — small bodies in distant, inclined and often retrograde orbits, believed to be captured fragments.

 

• Titan is Saturn's largest moon and the second largest moon in the solar system after Jupiter's Ganymede. It is the only moon known to have a dense atmosphere, composed mainly of nitrogen, and has lakes of liquid methane and ethane.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest. It is famous for its ring system, first observed by Galileo in 1610 and correctly explained by Christiaan Huygens. Its density is less than that of water, so it would float if a large enough ocean existed.

 

• The Cassini-Huygens mission, a joint venture of NASA, ESA and the Italian Space Agency, studied Saturn from 2004 to 2017; the Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005.

 

• Mercury and Venus have no moons. Mars has two — Phobos and Deimos.

 

NOTE

 

• Jupiter (Option 1): The largest planet, with about 95 IAU-recognised moons. Its four largest — Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto — are the Galilean moons, discovered by Galileo in 1610.

 

• Uranus (Option 3): Has about 28 known moons, named after characters in the works of Shakespeare and Pope.

 

• Neptune (Option 4): Has about 16 known moons, the largest being Triton, which orbits in a retrograde direction.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the Western Ghats?

I. The Western Ghats are geologically older than the Himalayas.

II. The Western Ghats run parallel to the western coast of India.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. The Western Ghats, also called the Sahyadri, are geologically older than the Himalayas and run parallel to the western coast of India. (पश्चिमी घाट — सह्याद्रि)

 

• Statement I is correct: the Western Ghats are a block mountain range formed by the faulting and uplift of the Deccan Plateau, and are estimated to be much older than the Himalayas, which are young fold mountains still rising today.

 

• Statement II is correct: the range runs roughly north to south for about 1,600 km, from the Tapi valley in the north to Kanyakumari in the south, passing through Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu, and lies parallel to the Arabian Sea coast.

 

• The Western Ghats are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2012) and one of the world's eight "hottest hotspots" of biological diversity. They intercept the south-west monsoon and cause heavy rainfall on their windward side, leaving a rain-shadow region to their east.

 

• The highest peak of the Western Ghats is Anamudi (2,695 m) in Kerala, which is also the highest peak of peninsular India. Doddabetta is the highest peak of the Nilgiris.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Important passes of the Western Ghats: Thal Ghat and Bhor Ghat in Maharashtra, and Palghat (Palakkad Gap) and Shencottah in Kerala. The Palghat Gap connects Kochi with Chennai.

 

• The major rivers rising in the Western Ghats — the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri — flow eastward into the Bay of Bengal, because the general slope of the peninsula is towards the east.

 

• The Eastern Ghats, by contrast, are discontinuous and eroded, being cut through by rivers. Their highest peak is Jindhagada in the Arma Konda range. The two Ghats meet at the Nilgiri Hills.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: The Square Kilometre Array (SKA), the largest radio telescope project in the world, is being built in South Africa and which other country?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Australia.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) is an international radio telescope project being constructed at two sites — in South Africa and in Australia. (स्क्वायर किलोमीटर एरे — दक्षिण अफ्रीका एवं ऑस्ट्रेलिया)

 

• SKA-Mid, the mid-frequency array of 197 dish antennas each 15 metres across, is being built in the Karoo desert of South Africa. SKA-Low, the low-frequency array of about 131,000 dipole antennas, is being built at the Murchison Radio-astronomy Observatory in Western Australia.

 

• The headquarters of the SKA Observatory (SKAO) is at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in the United Kingdom. Construction formally began in December 2022, and scientific operations are expected to begin towards the end of the decade.

 

• India is a member of the SKA Observatory, and the National Centre for Radio Astrophysics (NCRA), Pune, leads the Indian participation, particularly in developing the Telescope Manager software that will act as the "brain" of the observatory.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• India's own major radio telescope is the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (GMRT) at Khodad, near Narayangaon in Pune district, Maharashtra, consisting of 30 dish antennas of 45 metres diameter each. It was conceived by Prof. Govind Swarup, regarded as the father of radio astronomy in India.

 

• The Extremely Large Telescope (ELT), the world's largest optical telescope, is being built by the European Southern Observatory in the Atacama Desert of Chile.

 

NOTE

 

• Chile (Option 1): Host to major optical observatories such as the ELT, the VLT and the ALMA array, but not to the SKA.

 

• Canada (Option 3) and Japan (Option 4) are active in radio astronomy but are not SKA host countries.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding the reflection of sound?

I. An echo is heard when the reflected sound reaches the ear at least 0.1 second after the original sound.

II. Reverberation is the persistence of sound caused by its repeated reflection in a large enclosed space.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. (प्रतिध्वनि एवं अनुरणन)

 

• Statement I is correct: an echo is a distinctly repeated sound produced by reflection. The sensation of sound persists in the human ear for about 0.1 second, so the reflected sound must reach the ear at least 0.1 second after the direct sound to be heard separately.
◦ Taking the speed of sound in air as 344 m/s, the minimum distance of the reflecting surface works out to 344 × 0.1 ÷ 2 = 17.2 metres. The division by 2 is because the sound must travel to the obstacle and back.

 

• Statement II is correct: reverberation is the persistence of sound produced by repeated reflection from the walls, ceiling and floor of a large hall. Excessive reverberation makes speech unclear, which is why auditoriums are lined with sound-absorbing materials such as curtains, carpets, perforated boards and upholstered seats.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that requires a material medium to travel and therefore cannot travel through vacuum. Its speed is greatest in solids, less in liquids and least in gases — roughly 344 m/s in air at 22°C, about 1,500 m/s in water and about 5,960 m/s in steel.

 

• The audible range for human beings is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Below 20 Hz is infrasonic and above 20,000 Hz is ultrasonic. Bats, dolphins and porpoises use ultrasound for echolocation.

 

• Applications of the reflection of sound: SONAR (Sound Navigation and Ranging) for measuring the depth of the sea, stethoscope, megaphone, ultrasound scanning and the curved ceilings of concert halls.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are factually accurate.

question: Which of the following is the only major tidal port of India, situated on the Gulf of Kutch?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Deendayal (Kandla) Port.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Kandla Port, renamed the Deendayal Port in 2017 after Deendayal Upadhyaya, is India's only major tidal port, situated on the Gulf of Kutch in Gujarat. (दीनदयाल बंदरगाह — ज्वारीय पत्तन)

 

• A tidal port is one in which the movement of ships in and out of the harbour depends on the rise and fall of the tide, the high tide providing the depth of water required by large vessels.

 

• Kandla was developed after Partition in 1947, when Karachi went to Pakistan and western India lost its principal port. It serves a vast hinterland covering Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh and Jammu & Kashmir, and handles large volumes of petroleum, chemicals, fertilisers and salt. It is also known as the "Offshore Trading Hub" and has India's first Special Economic Zone, set up in 1965.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Distinctive features of Indian ports often asked in SSC:
◦ Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) — the deepest landlocked port; also India's oldest shipyard.
◦ Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Nhava Sheva), Maharashtra — the largest container port in India.
◦ Mumbai Port — a natural harbour and formerly the biggest port of India.
◦ Kolkata (Syama Prasad Mookerjee) Port — the only riverine major port, on the Hooghly.
◦ Paradip (Odisha) — a deep-water port exporting iron ore.
◦ Mormugao (Goa) — the leading iron-ore exporting port.
◦ Kochi (Kerala) — a natural harbour on the Willingdon Island.
◦ Ennore (Kamarajar) Port, Tamil Nadu — the first corporatised major port of India.
◦ Vizhinjam (Kerala) — India's first deep-water transhipment port.

 

• India has a coastline of about 7,516.6 km and handles roughly 95% of its trade by volume through sea routes.

 

NOTE

 

• Paradip Port (Option 1): In Odisha, at the confluence of the Mahanadi and the Bay of Bengal; not a tidal port.

 

• Chennai Port (Option 3): An artificial harbour and one of the oldest ports on the east coast.

 

• Mormugao Port (Option 4): In Goa, at the mouth of the Zuari river, chiefly an iron-ore port.

question: In which year was the first ICC Men's Cricket World Cup (One Day International) held?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1975.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The first ICC Men's Cricket World Cup was held in 1975 in England, and was then known as the Prudential Cup after its sponsor. (प्रथम क्रिकेट विश्व कप — 1975)

 

• West Indies won the tournament, defeating Australia in the final at Lord's. Clive Lloyd was the West Indies captain and scored 102 in the final. Matches in that edition were of 60 overs a side and were played in white clothing with a red ball.

 

• The first-ever One Day International had been played earlier, on 5 January 1971, between Australia and England at the Melbourne Cricket Ground.

 

• India won the World Cup in 1983 under Kapil Dev, defeating the West Indies at Lord's, and again in 2011 under M.S. Dhoni, defeating Sri Lanka at the Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai — the first time the final was won by a host nation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The first Men's T20 World Cup was held in 2007 in South Africa and was won by India under M.S. Dhoni, who also led India to the 2011 ODI World Cup and the 2013 Champions Trophy.

 

• The first Women's Cricket World Cup was held even earlier, in 1973 in England, two years before the men's tournament.

 

• The ICC was founded in 1909 as the Imperial Cricket Conference and has its headquarters at Dubai, UAE. Lord's in London is known as the Home of Cricket, and the Marylebone Cricket Club (MCC) is the custodian of the Laws of Cricket.

 

NOTE

 

• 1971 (Option 1): The year of the first One Day International match, not of the World Cup.

 

• 1979 (Option 3): The second World Cup, again held in England and won by the West Indies.

 

• 1983 (Option 4): The third World Cup, won by India under Kapil Dev.

question: At the COP-26 Climate Summit held at Glasgow in 2021, India committed to achieving a non-fossil fuel energy capacity of ______ by the year 2030.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 500 GW.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• At the COP-26 Climate Summit held at Glasgow in November 2021, Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a set of five commitments known as the "Panchamrit", of which the first was to raise India's non-fossil fuel energy capacity to 500 GW by 2030. (पंचामृत — 500 गीगावाट, 2030 तक)

 

• The five Panchamrit commitments are:
◦ Non-fossil fuel energy capacity of 500 GW by 2030
◦ Meeting 50% of energy requirements from renewable energy by 2030
◦ Reducing total projected carbon emissions by one billion tonnes by 2030
◦ Reducing the carbon intensity of the economy by 45% by 2030 from 2005 levels
◦ Achieving the target of net zero emissions by 2070

 

• India's earlier target, announced in 2015, had been 175 GW of renewable energy by 2022, comprising 100 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 10 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission was launched in 2010 as one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), which was itself announced in 2008.

 

• The National Green Hydrogen Mission was approved in January 2023 with an outlay of ₹19,744 crore, targeting 5 MMT of green hydrogen a year by 2030.

 

• The UNFCCC was adopted at the Rio Earth Summit, 1992; the Kyoto Protocol was signed in 1997; and the Paris Agreement was concluded at COP-21 in 2015, seeking to limit warming to well below 2°C and preferably 1.5°C.

 

NOTE

 

• 175 GW (Option 1): India's renewable energy target for 2022, not the 2030 non-fossil target.

 

• 300 GW (Option 2) and 450 GW (Option 3): 450 GW was an earlier figure announced at the UN Climate Action Summit in 2019, which was subsequently revised upward to 500 GW at Glasgow.

question: Which of the following books has been written by Amitav Ghosh?
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Hungry Tide.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "The Hungry Tide" (2004) was written by Amitav Ghosh. The novel is set in the Sundarbans of West Bengal and deals with the tension between conservation and the lives of the islanders. (द हंग्री टाइड — अमिताव घोष)

 

• Other well-known works of Amitav Ghosh: *The Circle of Reason, The Shadow Lines, The Calcutta Chromosome, The Glass Palace, River of Smoke, Flood of Fire, Gun Island* and *The Great Derangement*. *Sea of Poppies*, *River of Smoke* and *Flood of Fire* together form the Ibis Trilogy.

 

• Amitav Ghosh was awarded the Jnanpith Award in 2018, becoming the first Indian writer in English to receive it. He also won the Sahitya Akademi Award (1989) for *The Shadow Lines*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Indian authors who have won the Booker Prize: Salman Rushdie for *Midnight's Children* (1981), Arundhati Roy for *The God of Small Things* (1997), Kiran Desai for *The Inheritance of Loss* (2006) and Aravind Adiga for *The White Tiger* (2008). Geetanjali Shree won the International Booker Prize in 2022 for *Tomb of Sand* (*Ret Samadhi*), translated by Daisy Rockwell.

 

• V.S. Naipaul received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2001, and Rabindranath Tagore in 1913 for *Gitanjali*.

 

NOTE

 

• The God of Small Things (Option 2): Written by Arundhati Roy; won the Booker Prize in 1997.

 

• The Inheritance of Loss (Option 3): Written by Kiran Desai; won the Booker Prize in 2006.

 

• Interpreter of Maladies (Option 4): A collection of short stories by Jhumpa Lahiri; won the Pulitzer Prize in 2000.

question: The Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor (EDFC) of Indian Railways runs from Sahnewal near Ludhiana to which of the following?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sonnagar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Eastern Dedicated Freight Corridor (EDFC) runs from Sahnewal, near Ludhiana in Punjab, to Sonnagar in Bihar, a route length of about 1,337 km. (पूर्वी समर्पित माल गलियारा — 1,337 किमी)

 

• It passes through Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Jharkhand, and is designed principally to carry coal from the eastern coalfields to the thermal power plants of northern India, along with steel, cement and food grains. A part of it was financed by the World Bank.

 

• The Western Dedicated Freight Corridor (WDFC) runs from Dadri in Uttar Pradesh to the Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT) in Mumbai, a length of about 1,506 km, passing through Haryana, Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra. It is being built with Japanese (JICA) assistance and carries mainly container traffic.

 

• Both corridors are implemented by the Dedicated Freight Corridor Corporation of India Limited (DFCCIL), a public sector undertaking under the Ministry of Railways established in 2006, with headquarters at New Delhi.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The New Khurja–New Bhaupur section of the EDFC was the first to be dedicated to the nation, in December 2020. The Operation Control Centre of the EDFC is at Prayagraj, and that of the WDFC at Ahmedabad.

 

• Freight trains on the corridors run at a design speed of 100 km/h and can carry heavier axle loads than the Indian Railways network, greatly increasing capacity and reducing transit time.

 

• Additional corridors have been proposed, including the East-West, North-South, East Coast and South-West corridors.

 

NOTE

 

• Dadri (Option 2) and Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Option 3): These are the two ends of the Western DFC, not the Eastern.

 

• Visakhapatnam (Option 4): A major port on the east coast, but not a terminal of the EDFC.

question: Who is the author of the book 'India After Gandhi: The History of the World's Largest Democracy'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Ramachandra Guha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "India After Gandhi: The History of the World's Largest Democracy" (2007) was written by the historian Ramachandra Guha. (इंडिया आफ्टर गांधी — रामचंद्र गुहा)

 

• The book traces the political and social history of India from Independence in 1947 onwards, covering Partition, the integration of the princely states, the framing of the Constitution, the wars, the Emergency and the economic reforms.

 

• Other well-known works of Ramachandra Guha: *A Corner of a Foreign Field* (a social history of Indian cricket), *Gandhi Before India*, *Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World*, *Makers of Modern India*, *The Unquiet Woods* and *Environmentalism: A Global History*.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Well-known books on Indian history and politics frequently asked in SSC:
◦ *India's Struggle for Independence* — Bipan Chandra
◦ *The Idea of India* — Sunil Khilnani
◦ *The Discovery of India*, *Glimpses of World History* and *An Autobiography* — Jawaharlal Nehru
◦ *The Story of My Experiments with Truth* — Mahatma Gandhi
◦ *Waiting for a Visa* and *Annihilation of Caste* — B.R. Ambedkar
◦ *An Era of Darkness* and *The Great Indian Novel* — Shashi Tharoor
◦ *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India* — Dadabhai Naoroji
◦ *The Indian War of Independence, 1857* — V.D. Savarkar

 

NOTE

 

• Bipan Chandra (Option 1): Author of *India's Struggle for Independence* and *India Since Independence*.

 

• Sunil Khilnani (Option 2): Author of *The Idea of India* and *Incarnations: India in 50 Lives*.

 

• Shashi Tharoor (Option 3): Author of *An Era of Darkness*, *Why I Am a Hindu* and *The Great Indian Novel*.

question: Which of the following terms is NOT associated with the game of Badminton?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bull's eye.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• "Bull's eye" is not a badminton term. It refers to the centre of a target and is associated with archery and shooting, where hitting it scores the maximum points. (बुल्स आई — तीरंदाजी एवं निशानेबाजी)

 

• Terms genuinely used in badminton include: smash, drop shot, deuce, shuttlecock, service court, let, fault, rally, lob, drive, net shot, love all and match point.

 

• Badminton scoring: a match is the best of three games, each played to 21 points under the rally point system, in which a point is scored on every rally regardless of who served. If the score reaches 20-20, the game goes to deuce and a player must lead by two clear points; at 29-29, the player reaching 30 wins.

 

• The court measures 13.4 m × 6.1 m for doubles and 13.4 m × 5.18 m for singles, and the net is 1.55 m high at the posts.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• The international governing body is the Badminton World Federation (BWF), with headquarters at Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. Major team events are the Thomas Cup (men) and the Uber Cup (women).

 

• Indian achievements: Saina Nehwal won bronze at the 2012 London Olympics, the first Indian to win an Olympic medal in badminton; P.V. Sindhu won silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at Tokyo 2020, and became World Champion in 2019. Prakash Padukone won the All England Championship in 1980, and Pullela Gopichand in 2001. India won the Thomas Cup in 2022 for the first time.

 

NOTE

 

• Smash (Option 1): A powerful downward stroke played from above the head — badminton's most aggressive shot.

 

• Drop shot (Option 2): A soft stroke that just crosses the net and falls close to it.

 

• Deuce (Option 3): The situation at 20-20, when a lead of two points becomes necessary. The term is also used in tennis and table tennis.

question: The Narasimham Committee on Banking Sector Reforms, commonly called the Narasimham Committee II, submitted its report in which year?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1998.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Narasimham Committee II, formally the Committee on Banking Sector Reforms, was appointed in 1998 under the chairmanship of M. Narasimham, a former Governor of the Reserve Bank of India, and submitted its report in April 1998. (नरसिम्हम समिति-II — 1998)

 

• Its main recommendations were:
◦ Merger of strong banks to create three or four large banks of international character;
◦ Raising the Capital Adequacy Ratio to strengthen the capital base;
◦ Reduction of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs) to 3% by 2002 and the setting up of Asset Reconstruction Companies;
◦ Greater autonomy for public sector banks and a review of banking legislation;
◦ Introduction of the concept of narrow banking for weak banks.

 

• The Narasimham Committee I had been appointed in 1991, in the wake of the balance-of-payments crisis and the beginning of liberalisation. It recommended reducing the SLR and CRR, deregulating interest rates, prudential norms for income recognition and provisioning, and a four-tier banking structure. The Debt Recovery Tribunals were established following its recommendation.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other important committees in the financial sector:
◦ Malhotra Committee (1993) — insurance sector reforms, leading to the IRDA
◦ Chelliah Committee (1991) — tax reforms, including the rationalisation of import duties
◦ Rangarajan Committee — disinvestment, and later poverty estimation
◦ Vaghul Committee — money market reforms
◦ Nachiket Mor Committee (2013) — comprehensive financial services for small businesses and low-income households
◦ Bimal Jalan Committee (2019) — economic capital framework of the RBI

 

• The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission, and was nationalised on 1 January 1949. Its first Indian Governor was C.D. Deshmukh.

 

NOTE

 

• 1991 (Option 1): The year the Narasimham Committee I on the financial system was appointed.

 

• 1994 (Option 2) and 2001 (Option 4): Neither year is associated with the report of the Narasimham Committee II.

question: The Dilwara Jain Temples, renowned for their intricate marble carvings, are located in which Indian state?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rajasthan.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Dilwara Jain Temples are situated at Mount Abu in the Sirohi district of Rajasthan, in the Aravalli range, and are famous for their extraordinarily fine marble carving. (दिलवाड़ा जैन मंदिर — माउंट आबू, राजस्थान)

 

• They were built between the 11th and 13th centuries CE, largely under the patronage of the Solanki (Chalukya) rulers of Gujarat and their ministers. The complex has five temples:
◦ Vimal Vasahi — dedicated to Rishabhanatha (Adinatha), the first Tirthankara, built in 1031 CE by Vimal Shah, a minister of the Solanki ruler Bhimdev I. Its domed ceiling and the *Rang Mandap* are especially celebrated.
◦ Luna Vasahi — dedicated to Neminatha, the 22nd Tirthankara, built in 1230 CE by the brothers Vastupala and Tejpala.
◦ Pittalhar, Parshvanatha and Mahavir Swami temples.

 

• The marble is carved so thin in places that it is said to be translucent, and the ceilings, pillars and doorways are covered with lotus buds, dancers and figures from Jain mythology.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other important Jain sites: Shravanabelagola (Karnataka), with the Gommateshwara (Bahubali) statue where the Maha Mastakabhisheka is held; Palitana (Shatrunjaya) in Gujarat; Ranakpur in Rajasthan, famous for its 1,444 carved pillars; Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh, which has Jain temples alongside Hindu ones; and Girnar in Gujarat.

 

• Mount Abu is the only hill station of Rajasthan and the site of Guru Shikhar, the highest peak of the Aravallis at 1,722 metres. The Mount Abu Wildlife Sanctuary is also located there.

 

NOTE

 

• Gujarat (Option 1): Home to Palitana and Girnar, and to the Solanki dynasty that patronised the Dilwara temples, but the temples themselves are in Rajasthan.

 

• Madhya Pradesh (Option 3): Known for the Khajuraho group of temples, built by the Chandelas.

 

• Maharashtra (Option 4): Known for the Ajanta, Ellora and Elephanta cave complexes.

question: The Ajanta caves of Maharashtra are famous chiefly for which of the following?
option_1: Rock-cut Jain sculptures of the Tirthankaras
option_2: Mural paintings depicting the life and previous births of the Buddha
option_3: Bronze idols made during the Chola period
option_4: Frescoes painted during the reign of the Mughal emperors
solution_text:
The correct answer is Mural paintings depicting the life and previous births of the Buddha.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Ajanta caves, situated in the Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) district of Maharashtra, are celebrated above all for their mural paintings, which depict the life of the Buddha and the Jataka stories of his previous births. (अजंता — बौद्ध भित्तिचित्र)

 

• There are 30 caves, cut into a horseshoe-shaped cliff above the Waghora river, excavated in two phases — the earlier group belonging to the Satavahana period (2nd century BCE onwards) and the later and richer group to the Vakataka period (5th century CE), under the patronage of Harishena.

 

• The caves are of two kinds: Chaityas (prayer halls) and Viharas (monasteries). All the caves are Buddhist. The best-known paintings are the Bodhisattva Padmapani and Bodhisattva Vajrapani in Cave 1.

 

• The paintings were made in the fresco-secco technique, applied on a dry plaster surface. The caves were rediscovered in 1819 by a British officer, John Smith, during a hunting expedition, and were declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The nearby Ellora caves, also a UNESCO World Heritage Site, contain 34 caves representing three religions — Buddhist (1-12), Hindu (13-29) and Jain (30-34). The Kailasa Temple (Cave 16), carved out of a single rock by the Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna I, is the largest monolithic structure in the world.

 

• The Elephanta caves near Mumbai, dedicated to Lord Shiva and famous for the Trimurti sculpture, were built by the Rashtrakutas and are also a World Heritage Site.

 

NOTE

 

• Option 1 is incorrect — Jain caves are found at Ellora (caves 30-34) and Udayagiri-Khandagiri in Odisha, not at Ajanta.

 

• Option 3 is incorrect — Chola bronzes, such as the celebrated Nataraja, belong to Tamil Nadu and were made by the lost-wax (cire perdue) process.

 

• Option 4 is incorrect — the Ajanta paintings are far older than the Mughal period, belonging chiefly to the Satavahana and Vakataka eras.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are correct regarding Rutherford's model of the atom?

I. Most of the space inside an atom is empty.

II. The entire positive charge and almost the whole mass of an atom are concentrated in its nucleus.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both I and II.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Both statements are correct. They are the two principal conclusions drawn by Ernest Rutherford from his alpha-particle scattering experiment of 1911. (रदरफोर्ड का परमाणु मॉडल)

 

• In the experiment, a beam of alpha particles was directed at a thin gold foil. The observations and conclusions were:
◦ Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil → most of the space inside an atom is empty (Statement I).
◦ A few were deflected through small angles → there is a concentrated positive charge inside the atom that repels them.
◦ About one in 20,000 bounced straight back → the entire positive charge and nearly all the mass are concentrated in a very small volume, which Rutherford named the nucleus (Statement II).

 

• Rutherford estimated the radius of the nucleus to be about 10⁻¹⁵ m, roughly 10⁵ times smaller than the radius of the atom, which is about 10⁻¹⁰ m. He proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in circular orbits, and his model is therefore called the planetary model or nuclear model of the atom.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Drawback of Rutherford's model: according to classical electromagnetic theory, a charged particle moving in a circular orbit is accelerating and must continuously radiate energy. The electron would therefore spiral into the nucleus, making the atom unstable — which is not the case.

 

• This defect was removed by Niels Bohr (1913), who proposed that electrons revolve only in certain permitted discrete orbits (stationary states) without radiating energy, and that energy is emitted or absorbed only when an electron jumps from one orbit to another.

 

• J.J. Thomson's earlier model (1898) is called the plum pudding or watermelon model, in which electrons were embedded in a sphere of positive charge.

 

NOTE

 

• Options 1, 2 and 4 are incorrect, because both the given statements are correct conclusions of Rutherford's experiment.

question: The electron, the first subatomic particle to be discovered, was identified by which of the following scientists?
solution_text:
The correct answer is J.J. Thomson.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The electron was discovered by Sir J.J. Thomson in 1897 through his experiments with the cathode ray discharge tube. It was the first subatomic particle to be discovered. (इलेक्ट्रॉन — जे.जे. थॉमसन, 1897)

 

• Thomson showed that cathode rays consist of negatively charged particles that are identical whatever the gas or the electrode material used, proving that these particles are a universal constituent of all matter.

 

• Properties of the electron: charge −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ coulomb, mass 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg, which is about 1/1837 of the mass of a proton. The charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) was determined by Thomson, and the charge itself was measured by R.A. Millikan in his oil-drop experiment.

 

• Thomson received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1906.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Discovery of the three fundamental subatomic particles:
◦ Electron — J.J. Thomson (1897); charge −1, negligible mass
◦ Proton — Ernest Rutherford (1919), following work on anode/canal rays first observed by Eugen Goldstein (1886); charge +1, mass 1 u
◦ Neutron — James Chadwick (1932); no charge, mass 1 u

 

• The atomic number (Z) is the number of protons, and the mass number (A) the total number of protons and neutrons. Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers, isobars the same mass number but different atomic numbers, and isotones the same number of neutrons.

 

NOTE

 

• Ernest Rutherford (Option 2): Discovered the proton and the nucleus; called the father of nuclear physics.

 

• Niels Bohr (Option 3): Proposed the model of discrete electron orbits in 1913; Nobel Prize 1922.

 

• Eugen Goldstein (Option 4): Discovered canal rays (anode rays) in 1886, which led to the identification of the proton, but he did not discover the electron.

question: Avani Lekhara, who won a gold medal at the Paralympic Games, is associated with which sport?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Shooting.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Avani Lekhara is an Indian para-shooter from Jaipur, Rajasthan. (अवनि लेखरा — पैरा निशानेबाजी)

 

• At the Tokyo 2020 Paralympic Games (held in 2021) she won gold in the women's 10 m Air Rifle Standing SH1 event, becoming the first Indian woman to win a Paralympic gold medal, and added a bronze in the 50 m Rifle 3 Positions SH1. At the Paris 2024 Paralympics she retained her 10 m Air Rifle Standing SH1 title, becoming the first Indian woman to win two Paralympic golds.

 

• She was left with a spinal cord injury after a car accident in 2012 and took up shooting in 2015, drawing inspiration from Abhinav Bindra's autobiography *A Shot at History*.

 

• She has been honoured with the Khel Ratna and the Padma Shri.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Other prominent Indian para-athletes:
◦ Sumit Antil — javelin throw (F64); gold at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024
◦ Devendra Jhajharia — javelin throw; India's first para-athlete to win two Paralympic golds (2004 and 2016)
◦ Pramod Bhagat — para-badminton; gold at Tokyo 2020
◦ Murlikant Petkar — swimming; India's first Paralympic gold medallist, at Heidelberg in 1972
◦ Mariyappan Thangavelu — high jump; gold at Rio 2016
◦ Deepa Malik — shot put; first Indian woman to win a Paralympic medal, at Rio 2016

 

• Abhinav Bindra won India's first individual Olympic gold in 10 m Air Rifle at Beijing 2008. Manu Bhaker became the first Indian to win two medals at a single Olympics, at Paris 2024.

 

NOTE

 

• Archery (Option 1): Indian para-archers include Harvinder Singh, who won gold at Paris 2024.

 

• Para-athletics (Option 3): Covers track and field events such as javelin, high jump and discus.

 

• Para-swimming (Option 4): The discipline in which Murlikant Petkar won India's first Paralympic gold in 1972.
